related_questions.question: What actions should be taken when a carbon monoxide leak occurs?

text_blocks.snippet: If you suspect a carbon monoxide leak, immediately evacuate the premises and seek fresh air. Call emergency services (911) or your local gas company to report the leak and get assistance. Do not re-enter the building until it has been deemed safe by professionals.
snippet_highlighted_words: immediately evacuate the premises and seek fresh air

list.title: Leave the area:
list.snippet: If you suspect a carbon monoxide leak, get everyone out of the building and into fresh air immediately.

list.title: Call for help:
list.snippet: Contact emergency services (911) or your local gas company (e.g., PGE in California).

list.title: Don't re-enter:
list.snippet: Avoid going back inside until the area is declared safe by first responders or gas company personnel.

text_blocks.snippet: 2. What to do if you are feeling symptoms:

list.title: Seek medical attention:
list.snippet: If you or anyone else is experiencing symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning (headache, dizziness, nausea, shortness of breath, etc.), go to the nearest emergency room or seek immediate medical help.

list.title: Be prepared to answer questions:
list.snippet: The medical team may ask about the possible source of the leak, your symptoms, and other relevant information.

list.title: Install CO detectors:
list.snippet: Carbon monoxide detectors are crucial for early detection of leaks. Install them outside each sleeping area and on every level of your home.

list.title: Test detectors regularly:
list.snippet: Test CO detectors monthly and replace batteries as needed.

list.title: Maintain appliances:
list.snippet: Have all fuel-burning appliances (furnaces, water heaters, stoves, etc.) regularly inspected and maintained by qualified professionals, according to Manitoba Hydro.

list.title: Proper ventilation:
list.snippet: Ensure proper ventilation for fuel-burning appliances and avoid using them in enclosed spaces (e.g., never run a car or generator in a garage).

list.title: Be aware of symptoms:
list.snippet: Familiarize yourself with the symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning and seek medical attention if you experience any.

related_questions.question: How to respond to a carbon monoxide alarm?

text_blocks.snippet: If a carbon monoxide alarm sounds, immediately evacuate everyone from the building to fresh air and call 911 from a safe location outside. Do not re-enter the building until emergency responders have checked for the source of the carbon monoxide and deemed it safe. If anyone is experiencing symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning, such as headache, dizziness, or nausea, inform the emergency responders immediately.
snippet_highlighted_words: immediately evacuate everyone from the building to fresh air and call 911 from a safe location outside

list.snippet: Don't wait to investigate the cause of the alarm.
Get everyone, including pets, out of the building and into fresh air.
Open windows and doors as you leave, if it's safe to do so, to help ventilate the area.
Call 911 from outside the building, or from a neighbor's home.
Inform the operator that a carbon monoxide alarm has gone off and if anyone is experiencing symptoms.
Do not go back inside until emergency responders have arrived, assessed the situation, and declared it safe.
Even if the alarm stops, there could still be dangerous levels of carbon monoxide present.

text_blocks.snippet: 4. Identify and Address the Source (After the Incident):

list.snippet: Once the situation is under control, have a qualified technician inspect any fuel-burning appliances (furnace, water heater, etc.) and chimneys.
Ensure that any potential sources of carbon monoxide are properly installed, maintained, and ventilated.
Install carbon monoxide detectors on each level of your home, particularly near sleeping areas.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions for installation, maintenance, and battery replacement.
Never use a gas range or oven to heat your home, and avoid running vehicles or gas-powered equipment in enclosed spaces.

related_questions.question: What are the requirements for NFPA 72 carbon monoxide?

text_blocks.snippet: NFPA 72, the National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, mandates carbon monoxide (CO) detection in various locations, including habitable levels, sleeping areas, and near fuel-burning appliances. These requirements are designed to protect occupants from the dangers of CO poisoning, which can result from fuel-burning appliances, generators, or vehicles.

list.title: Location:
list.snippet: CO detectors should be placed on every habitable level, centrally located in HVAC zones, and within 21 feet of each sleeping area's door. They should also be located near fuel-burning appliances, generally within 1 to 3 meters horizontally from the appliance and between the appliance's height and 150mm below the ceiling, according to Safelincs, not above a stove, notes Safelincs.

list.title: Power Source:
list.snippet: CO alarms should be powered by the building's wiring with battery backup, or be battery-powered in buildings without electricity, according to UpCodes.

list.title: Testing and Maintenance:
list.snippet: Regular testing and maintenance are crucial. This includes visual inspections semi-annually, functional tests annually, and system testing every three years by a qualified service technician. Batteries should be replaced on the manufacturer's recommended schedule, and the entire device should be replaced when it reaches the end of its lifespan, according to QRFS.

list.title: Interconnection:
list.snippet: In many jurisdictions, CO detectors are required to be interconnected, meaning when one alarm is triggered, all alarms in the system will sound, according to Rhode Island Government.

list.title: Listing:
list.snippet: CO detectors must be listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, such as UL, and comply with standards like UL 2034 for single-station alarms or UL 2075 for those connected to a system, according to UpCodes.

list.title: Fuel-Burning Appliances:
list.snippet: CO detection is particularly important near fuel-burning appliances like furnaces, fireplaces, and water heaters.

list.title: Sleeping Areas:
list.snippet: CO detectors are essential in or near sleeping areas to provide early warning during the night, according to the City of Portland.

list.title: Residential and Commercial:
list.snippet: Requirements can vary between residential and commercial settings, with commercial systems often involving a central control panel, notes cdn.ymaws.com.

list.title: Building Codes:
list.snippet: It's crucial to consult the specific building codes adopted in your area, as they may have additional or more stringent requirements than NFPA 72 alone, says Electrical Contractor Magazine.

text_blocks.snippet: NFPA 72 also addresses CO detection systems in the context of mass notification systems for various emergencies, highlighting the evolving role of CO detection in broader safety strategies.
